title: Review: The human nervous system; Hormonal coordination in humans
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for AQA GCSE Biology (8461) (status of the source: authored-gated-unreviewed). Terms and clues: 4.5.2-c19 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.5.2-c11 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.5.2-c13 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.5.2-c12 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: 4.5.2-q07, 4.5.2-q09, 4.5.2-q13, 4.5.3-q03, 4.5.3-q06, 4.5.2-q10, 4.5.3-q01, 4.5.3-q07, 4.5.2-q12, 4.5.3-q02, 4.5.3-q05, 4.5.2-q11. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Myopia (short sightedness)
items.clue: A defect of the eye in which rays of light from a distant object focus in front of the retina.

items.label: Cerebral cortex
items.clue: The outer, folded region of the brain, responsible for consciousness, intelligence, memory and language.

items.label: Medulla
items.clue: The region of the brain stem that controls unconscious activities such as heart rate and breathing rate.

items.label: Cerebellum
items.clue: The region at the back and base of the brain, responsible for coordinating muscular activity and balance.

questions.stem: A patient can no longer coordinate their movements or keep their balance after an injury to the brain. Which is the most likely cause?

options.text: Damage within the medulla
The cerebellum is damaged
Cerebral cortex is damaged
Damage to the spinal cord

questions.explanation: The cerebellum is the region of the brain responsible for coordinating muscular activity and balance, which are the functions the patient has lost.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly relates a structure of the eye to its function?

options.text: The cornea changes shape to focus images.
The iris narrows the pupil in dim lighting.
The ciliary muscles relax for near objects.
The retina contains receptors for light.

questions.explanation: The eye is a sense organ containing receptors sensitive to light intensity and colour, and these receptors are found in the retina at the back of the eye.

questions.stem: A person is exercising hard and their body temperature rises above normal. What happens in the skin?

options.text: Blood vessels dilate and sweat is produced.
Blood vessels move nearer the skin surface.
Blood vessels constrict and shivering starts.
The skin cools the body without the brain.

questions.explanation: If the body temperature is too high, blood vessels dilate (vasodilation) and sweat is produced from the sweat glands; both mechanisms cause a transfer of energy from the skin to the environment.

questions.stem: Why is the pituitary gland described as a 'master gland'?

options.text: its hormones make other glands release hormones
its hormones produce all the body effects directly
its hormones travel to the glands along nerves
its hormones act on every organ in the body

questions.explanation: The pituitary gland secretes several hormones into the blood in response to body conditions, and these act on other glands to stimulate other hormones to be released.

options.text: the body cells no longer respond to insulin
the pancreas releases insulin when glucose is low
the pancreas fails to produce enough insulin
the pancreas is affected by a person's diet

questions.explanation: Type 1 diabetes is a disorder in which the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin, and it is characterised by uncontrolled high blood glucose levels.

questions.stem: A person walks out of bright sunlight into a dark room. What happens in the eye?

options.text: The iris muscles make the pupil narrower.
The ciliary muscles make the lens thicker.
The cornea changes shape to admit light.
The iris muscles make the pupil wider.

questions.explanation: The eye adapts to dim light by the iris muscles widening the pupil, so more light enters the eye and reaches the receptors in the retina.

questions.stem: A gland of the endocrine system secretes a hormone. How does that hormone reach the organ where it produces an effect, and how do its effects compare with those of the nervous system?

options.text: carried along nerves; effects are slower but last longer
carried in the blood; effects are faster but end much sooner
carried along nerves; effects are faster but end sooner
carried in the blood; effects are slower but last longer

questions.explanation: Glands secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream and the blood carries the hormone to a target organ; compared to the nervous system the effects are slower but act for longer.

questions.stem: A person with Type 2 diabetes has a normal concentration of insulin in the blood but a high blood glucose concentration. Why?

options.text: their pancreas has completely stopped making insulin
their insulin cannot act on glucose in the blood
their body cells no longer respond to insulin
their insulin is released when blood glucose is low

questions.explanation: In Type 2 diabetes the body cells no longer respond to insulin produced by the pancreas, so glucose is not moved from the blood into the cells even though insulin is present.

questions.stem: A ray diagram shows light from a distant object coming to a focus in front of the retina. Which defect is shown, and how is it corrected?

options.text: Myopia, corrected with a convex lens.
Hyperopia, corrected with a convex lens.
Myopia, corrected with a concave lens.
Hyperopia, corrected with a concave lens.

questions.explanation: Rays focusing in front of the retina show myopia (short sightedness); a concave spectacle lens spreads the rays out so that they do focus on the retina.

questions.stem: A student labels endocrine glands on a diagram of the human body. Which label has been placed in the correct position?

options.text: the adrenal gland labelled inside the brain
the thyroid gland labelled in the lower neck
the pituitary gland labelled below the stomach
the pancreas labelled at the base of the brain

questions.explanation: The thyroid is found in the neck, and students should be able to identify its position on a diagram of the human body.

questions.stem: A person's blood glucose concentration is too high. What happens to the excess glucose?

options.text: it is changed into glycogen in the blood
it is released from the cells into the blood
it is changed into glycogen in the pancreas
it moves into cells and is stored as glycogen

questions.explanation: Insulin causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells, and in liver and muscle cells excess glucose is converted to glycogen for storage.

questions.stem: A student looks up from a book and focuses on a tree in the distance. What happens in the eye?

options.text: The ciliary muscles contract and the lens thickens.
The suspensory ligaments loosen and the lens bulges.
The cornea changes shape and the lens stays thin.
The ciliary muscles relax and the lens is pulled thin.

questions.explanation: To focus on a distant object the ciliary muscles relax, the suspensory ligaments are pulled tight and the lens is pulled thin, so it only slightly refracts the light rays.
